title: Digital enablers and building blocks for collaborative Earth Observation and Satellite telecommunications for Space solutions (Space Partnership)
destinationDetails:
Today, EU citizens enjoy watching satellite TV, increasingly accurate global navigation services for all transport modes and users, extended Earth monitoring for land, marine, atmosphere and climate change, global meteorological observation and accurate cartographies of a wide number of variables. Space also makes important contributions to security crisis management and emergency services. The EU Space Programme components (such as EGNSS and Copernicus) are key assets for the EU policies on climate, environment, transport, agriculture and secure society. Finally, the Space sector is a source of economic growth and jobs.

This Destination is structured along the following building blocks:

  • Accessing Space, i.e. the ability to transport satellites, cargo, and humans into space; build and launch the required vehicles, including re-usable systems; and operate the related facilities and services.
  • Using Space on Earth, i.e. the ability to provide space-based secure communication, navigation and Earth observation services and applications, including through the EU Space flagships Galileo, Copernicus and IRIS2.
  • Monitoring Space, i.e. the ability to detect, track and anticipate the trajectory of spacecraft, Near-Earth objects, and space debris during their full lifetime; to share data with relevant stakeholders; and to provide solutions for safe international space traffic management. It also includes the tracking and anticipation of other impacts on the space environment, such as Space weather events.
  • Acting in Space, i.e. the ability to inspect, rendezvous and dock, grasp, repair, refuel, reconfigure, build, assemble and disassemble, reuse/recycle, relocate, remove and transport operational, non-operational, and other objects in space, including platforms or larger structures.
  • Exploring Space, i.e. the ability to conduct high profile space exploration activities, perform excellent science and exploit space data to increase our knowledge about the Universe and celestial bodies, with a view to their exploration for scientific and socio-economic benefits.
  • Boosting Space, i.e. the ability to sustain the above strategic capabilities through fostering the competitiveness of the EU space sector; improving education and developing the required skills; accelerating the pace of innovation; supporting EU non-dependency on critical technologies; and strengthening international cooperation.

Those building blocks are implemented through the following headings:

  • Heading 1: Accessing Space

Autonomous access to space is a prerequisite for the strategic autonomy of the EU. It is a key enabler and indispensable element in the space ecosystem and value chain. European launch systems allow the autonomous deployment of satellites for the Union’s flagships Copernicus, Galileo/EGNOS and IRIS2 and contribute to the security and resilience of Europe’s sovereign space infrastructure.

In a context of fierce competition and launch services paradigm changes, ensuring that Europe improves the resilience and the cost-effectiveness of its autonomous access to space is crucial. This requires urgent activities to enable and further consolidate operational capacities before 2030 in line with the Strategic R&I Agenda for EU-funded Space research supporting competitiveness adopted in 2020.

This challenge will be tackled by fostering space transportation solutions through the support to building blocks for smart technologies and digital solutions and through facilitating access to European spaceports.

  • Heading 2: Acting in Space

In-Space Operations and Services (ISOS) will ensure EU’s freedom of action in space and increase the resilience, sustainability, safety and protection of its space infrastructure, and contribute to the strengthening of the competitiveness of its space sector. R&I activities should bring Europe to the forefront of emerging service applications, including inspection, rendezvous and docking, grasping, repair, reconfiguration, assembly and disassembly, manufacturing, resource extraction, reuse/recycling, removal and transport of objects in space, for satellites, platforms and larger structures. Key space R&I activities will be driven by a pilot mission that will contribute to establish and foster a new in-space economy.

Game-changing innovations and enabling technologies are at the heart of ISOS and an important focus of future actions. The paradigm shift towards adaptive space systems builds on automation and robotics, artificial intelligence, modular and reconfigurable spacecraft concepts. Together with other enabling technologies such as electric propulsion, intelligent mechanisms and interfaces or advanced GNC, they will provide new ways on how space assets are designed, produced, tested, transported, and operated. Different means realised with AppStore-like approaches will benefit the future space ecosystem and foster a circular economy.

  • Heading 3: Using Space on Earth related to telecommunications

The Union Secure Connectivity programme aims to develop a secure and autonomous space-based connectivity system for the provision of guaranteed and resilient satellite communications on Earth. Among the objectives are to develop, build and operate a multiorbital space-based state-of-the-art connectivity system, continuously adapted to governmental satellite communications demand evolution; to complement the Union pool of satellite communication capacities and services; and to integrate the GOVSATCOM ground segment infrastructure, as well as the European quantum communication infrastructure (EuroQCI).

In the context of the co-Programmed European Partnership for Globally Competitive Space Systems (Space Partnership), R&I will focus on cohesive activities in the domain of digital developments under the grand heading of Digitalisation for Commercial Space solutions, more specifically on collaborative and synergetic solutions for Earth Observation and Satellite Telecommunication missions.

  • Heading 4: Using Space on Earth related to Earth Observation

The evolution of Copernicus core services (Climate Change, Marine Environment Monitoring, Land Monitoring, Atmosphere Monitoring, Emergency Management and Security) is being taken care of through projects launched under the previous R&I work programmes.

In the context of the co-Programmed European Partnership for Globally Competitive Space Systems (Space Partnership), R&I will focus on cohesive activities in the domain of digital developments under the grand heading of Digitalisation for Commercial Space solutions, more specifically on collaborative and synergetic solutions for Earth Observation and Satellite Telecommunication missions.

In addition, we will strive to also support the development of innovative applications of Copernicus’ services and data. That said, such support is also coming from non-HE activities carried out by EUSPA, the EU agency for the Space Programme: collaboration with receivers’ manufacturers, with mobile phones’ manufacturers, with cars’ manufacturers, etc., as well as through influencing the development of policies where the use of Earth Observation data is required.

  • Heading 5: Using Space on Earth related to satellite navigation

For Galileo/EGNOS, the international context, the competitive environment with emerging actors including from the private sector, novel techniques in the value chain such as LEO layer for PNT or ground segment automation based on Artificial Intelligence, the increasing threats in space and in cyber, and the evolution of the technologies, components and systems, call for a constant adaptation of the EU space infrastructure to these changing realities.

To meet these challenges, EU needs sustained investments in R&D for innovative mission concepts, technology and systems. These will ensure the continuity of the EGNSS service, minimise the risks for technology inclusion in the infrastructure, thanks to anticipated development and testing including in-orbit, and protect better this infrastructure against modern threats (notably cyber, jamming/spoofing, natural hazards).

These investments in R&D will contribute to maintaining the EU´s leadership position in the Global Navigation Satellite Systems, and to strengthening the strategic autonomy of the EU.

In addition, we will strive to also support the development of innovative applications of EGNSS’ services and data. That said, such support is also coming from non-HE activities carried out by EUSPA, the EU agency for the Space Programme: collaboration with receivers’ manufacturers, with mobile phones’ manufacturers, with cars’ manufacturers, etc., as well as through influencing the development of policies where the use of satellite navigation data is required.

  • Heading 6: Space sciences and exploration

Space sciences and exploration are important areas that must be fostered for various reasons, focusing on where the EU can add value with limited financial means. Firstly, it is key to capitalise on Europe’s investments in space missions and exploit data coming from European space missions (including demonstration and validation). This should lay the grounds for future exploration missions. Furthermore, such focus on sciences will strengthen the position of leading European scientists and also animate societal interest in space. Last but not least, it will expand human knowledge and the natural curiosity of mankind.

  • Heading 7: Monitoring Space

Orbital space infrastructure, the data, and the services they deliver have become indispensable for European societies and economies and in the daily lives of Europeans. However, due to an increasingly congested orbital space, the likelihood of a satellite being severely damaged or destroyed in a collision has raised dramatically. Such risk calls for action to preserve European interests by protecting its private and public investments in space in a sustainable manner.

Based on the EU Space Programme, capabilities of the Space Situational Awareness (SSA) component and Space Surveillance and Tracking (SST) services are being developed and consolidated through a Partnership of 15 Member States. The EU SST Partnership Agreement has entered into force on 11 November 2022. With this Partnership, EU SST builds on the good results achieved by the initial consortium of 5 Member States and targets continuity of activities and service provision, improvement of specialisation on expertise, and consideration of the duality and security dimension of SST.

EU SST relies on the European industry, including start-ups, to develop and improve national, public-owned capacities based on Partnership’s requirements. In the pursuit of EU strategic autonomy, both as regards the need to protect EU space infrastructures and as regards the need to strengthen EU SST capabilities, research and development activities are aiming the enhancement and consolidation of EU SST autonomy in all orbital zones beyond the existing network of national assets, counting on MS contributions and leveraging complementary contributions from European private capabilities and commercial initiatives.

Importantly, SSA also covers the domains of Space Weather (SW) and Near-Earth Objects (NEO). For those domains, activities are ongoing and no additional ones are needed under the 2026-2027 WP.

  • Heading 8: Boosting space through EU non-dependence for key critical space technologies

Ensuring non-dependence for critical space technologies is key, especially in the current geo-political context. The European Commission has undertaken several activities and deployed new tools (e.g. the EU Observatory of Critical Technologies) for assessing space technologies and identify those that are critical from a dependency point of view. Within this domain, a number of technological developments will be initiated with focus on priorities stemming from on-going and planned EU Space missions, including IRIS2. Emphasis will be on reducing non-EU dependencies on critical space technologies across their whole supply chain from advanced materials to components, equipment, and sub-systems; providing unrestricted access to advanced space technologies relevant for EU space missions and programme components; developing or regaining capacity to operate independently in space by developing resilient space technologies supply chains, relying on EU supply chains and/or trustable and reliable supply chains not affected by non-EU export restrictions; enhancing competitiveness by developing products and capabilities reaching equivalent or superior performance level than those from outside the EU and compete at worldwide level; and opening new opportunities for manufacturers by reducing dependency on export restricted technologies.

  • Heading 9: Boosting Space through innovative space technologies

Mastering quantum technologies is essential for EU technological sovereignty and their use in EU space missions will offer major improvements in the performance of the EU space systems. Their developments will contribute to EU leadership in this field, in particular quantum sensing technology based on quantum accelerometers, developed in the frame of the Quantum Space Gravimetry pathfinder mission.

  • Heading 10: Boosting Space through IOD/IOV opportunities

IOD/IOV opportunities continue to be needed for experiments needing aggregation as well as for read-to-fly satellites. This includes the Flight Ticket Initiative to support competitiveness and innovation of the European Space sector.

  • Heading 11: Boosting Space through support to entrepreneurship

Business development, acceleration and upscaling of start-ups is also much needed, which has given rise to the set-up of the CASSINI Space Entrepreneurship Initiative. CASSINI provides support to business and innovation-friendly ecosystems, including the strengthening business skills in the space market segments and digital services based on space data. CASSINI also aims at making start-ups and scale-ups investment-ready and able to secure venture capital funding and at leveraging synergies with the InvestEU programme and the EU Space Programme.

  • Heading 12: Boosting Space through support to the Space Act and cybersecurity

The interinstitutional discussions for the adoption of an EU Space Act will start as soon as the Commission has issued its proposal still in 2025. One adopted, it will be important to foresee some studies and assimilated activities to support its implementation. The same goes for the area of cybersecurity which has become extremely important also in the Space domain.

Limiting participation in certain actions to Member States (and certain associated countries to Horizon Europe)

The Space research part of the Horizon Europe Programme is by default open to the world, promoting international cooperation to drive scientific excellence.

However, an important aspect of this Destination consists in ensuring security and strengthening strategic autonomy across key technologies and value chains, taking advantage of the possibilities that space offers for the security of the Union and its Member States. This objective requires special rules in specific cases to set the requisite eligibility and participation conditions to ensure the protection of the integrity, security and resilience of the Union and its Member States. Hence, on an exceptional basis and duly justified, this work programme may foresee a limited participation to entities from selected countries. Such exceptional circumstances would relate to prevalent considerations to safeguard the Union’s strategic assets, interests, autonomy or security. Possibilities for such limitations are framed by Article 22(5) of the Horizon Europe Regulation.

Legal entities established in China are not eligible to participate in both Research and Innovation Actions (RIAs) and Innovation Actions (IAs) falling under this Destination. For additional information please see “Restrictions on the participation of legal entities established in China” found in General Annex B of the General Annexes.

Furthermore, proposed activities should be complementary to H2020 and Horizon Europe funded projects, national activities and activities funded by the European Space Agency (ESA).

This topic contributes to the implementation of the European Partnership on ‘Globally Competitive Space Systems’ (GCSS).

In this topic, the integration of the gender dimension (sex and gender analysis) in research and innovation content should be addressed only if relevant in relation to the objectives of the research effort.

2. Eligible Countries

described in Annex B of the Work Programme General Annexes.

A number of non-EU/non-Associated Countries that are not automatically eligible for funding have made specific provisions for making funding available for their participants in Horizon Europe projects. See the information in the Horizon Europe Programme Guide.

3. Other Eligible Conditions

If projects use satellite-based earth observation, positioning, navigation and/or related timing data and services, beneficiaries must make use of Copernicus and/or Galileo/EGNOS (other data and services may additionally be used).

In order to achieve the expected outcomes, and safeguard the Union’s strategic assets, interests, autonomy, and security, it is important to avoid a situation of technological dependency on a non-EU source, in a global context that requires the EU to take action to build on its strengths, and to carefully assess and address any strategic weaknesses, vulnerabilities and high-risk dependencies which put at risk the attainment of its ambitions. For this reason, participation is limited to legal entities established in Member States, Iceland and Norway and the following additional associated countries : Canada, New-Zealand, United Kingdom and Switzerland. In addition, entities established in third countries which may become associated to Horizon Europe during 2026 and 2027 may be eligible to participate in this topic if the third country is identified for this topic as an eligible country in the List of Participating Countries in Horizon Europe at the time of submission of the application[[See the List of Participating Countries in Horizon Europe available at https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/common/guidance/list-3rd-country-participation_horizon-euratom_en.pdf.]]. In any case, the association agreement to the Programme must apply by the time of the signature of the grant agreement.

For the duly justified and exceptional reasons listed in the paragraph above, in order to guarantee the protection of the strategic interests of the Union and its Member States, entities established in an eligible country listed above, but which are directly or indirectly controlled by a non-eligible country or by a non-eligible country entity, may not participate in the action unless it can be demonstrated, by means of guarantees positively assessed by their eligible country of establishment, that their participation to the action would not negatively impact the Union’s strategic assets, interests, autonomy, or security. Entities assessed as high-risk suppliers of mobile network communication equipment within the meaning of ‘restrictions for the protection of European communication networks’ (or entities fully or partially owned or controlled by a high-risk supplier) cannot submit guarantees.[[ The guarantees shall in particular substantiate that, for the purpose of the action, measures are in place to ensure that: a) control over the applicant legal entity is not exercised in a manner that retrains or restricts its ability to carry out the action and to deliver results, that imposes restrictions concerning its infrastructure, facilities, assets, resources, intellectual property or know-how needed for the purpose of the action, or that undermines its capabilities and standards necessary to carry out the action; b) access by a non-eligible country or by a non-eligible country entity to sensitive information relating to the action is prevented; and the employees or other persons involved in the action have a national security clearance issued by an eligible country, where appropriate; c) ownership of the intellectual property arising from, and the results of, the action remain within the recipient during and after completion of the action, are not subject to control or restrictions by non-eligible countries or non-eligible country entity, and are not exported outside the eligible countries, nor is access to them from outside the eligible countries granted, without the approval of the eligible country in which the legal entity is established.]]

title: Digital enablers and building blocks for collaborative Earth Observation and Satellite telecommunications for Space solutions (Space Partnership)
destinationDetails:
Today, EU citizens enjoy watching satellite TV, increasingly accurate global navigation services for all transport modes and users, extended Earth monitoring for land, marine, atmosphere and climate change, global meteorological observation and accurate cartographies of a wide number of variables. Space also makes important contributions to security crisis management and emergency services. The EU Space Programme components (such as EGNSS and Copernicus) are key assets for the EU policies on climate, environment, transport, agriculture and secure society. Finally, the Space sector is a source of economic growth and jobs.

This Destination is structured along the following building blocks:

  • Accessing Space, i.e. the ability to transport satellites, cargo, and humans into space; build and launch the required vehicles, including re-usable systems; and operate the related facilities and services.
  • Using Space on Earth, i.e. the ability to provide space-based secure communication, navigation and Earth observation services and applications, including through the EU Space flagships Galileo, Copernicus and IRIS2.
  • Monitoring Space, i.e. the ability to detect, track and anticipate the trajectory of spacecraft, Near-Earth objects, and space debris during their full lifetime; to share data with relevant stakeholders; and to provide solutions for safe international space traffic management. It also includes the tracking and anticipation of other impacts on the space environment, such as Space weather events.
  • Acting in Space, i.e. the ability to inspect, rendezvous and dock, grasp, repair, refuel, reconfigure, build, assemble and disassemble, reuse/recycle, relocate, remove and transport operational, non-operational, and other objects in space, including platforms or larger structures.
  • Exploring Space, i.e. the ability to conduct high profile space exploration activities, perform excellent science and exploit space data to increase our knowledge about the Universe and celestial bodies, with a view to their exploration for scientific and socio-economic benefits.
  • Boosting Space, i.e. the ability to sustain the above strategic capabilities through fostering the competitiveness of the EU space sector; improving education and developing the required skills; accelerating the pace of innovation; supporting EU non-dependency on critical technologies; and strengthening international cooperation.

Those building blocks are implemented through the following headings:

  • Heading 1: Accessing Space

Autonomous access to space is a prerequisite for the strategic autonomy of the EU. It is a key enabler and indispensable element in the space ecosystem and value chain. European launch systems allow the autonomous deployment of satellites for the Union’s flagships Copernicus, Galileo/EGNOS and IRIS2 and contribute to the security and resilience of Europe’s sovereign space infrastructure.

In a context of fierce competition and launch services paradigm changes, ensuring that Europe improves the resilience and the cost-effectiveness of its autonomous access to space is crucial. This requires urgent activities to enable and further consolidate operational capacities before 2030 in line with the Strategic R&I Agenda for EU-funded Space research supporting competitiveness adopted in 2020.

This challenge will be tackled by fostering space transportation solutions through the support to building blocks for smart technologies and digital solutions and through facilitating access to European spaceports.

  • Heading 2: Acting in Space

In-Space Operations and Services (ISOS) will ensure EU’s freedom of action in space and increase the resilience, sustainability, safety and protection of its space infrastructure, and contribute to the strengthening of the competitiveness of its space sector. R&I activities should bring Europe to the forefront of emerging service applications, including inspection, rendezvous and docking, grasping, repair, reconfiguration, assembly and disassembly, manufacturing, resource extraction, reuse/recycling, removal and transport of objects in space, for satellites, platforms and larger structures. Key space R&I activities will be driven by a pilot mission that will contribute to establish and foster a new in-space economy.

Game-changing innovations and enabling technologies are at the heart of ISOS and an important focus of future actions. The paradigm shift towards adaptive space systems builds on automation and robotics, artificial intelligence, modular and reconfigurable spacecraft concepts. Together with other enabling technologies such as electric propulsion, intelligent mechanisms and interfaces or advanced GNC, they will provide new ways on how space assets are designed, produced, tested, transported, and operated. Different means realised with AppStore-like approaches will benefit the future space ecosystem and foster a circular economy.

  • Heading 3: Using Space on Earth related to telecommunications

The Union Secure Connectivity programme aims to develop a secure and autonomous space-based connectivity system for the provision of guaranteed and resilient satellite communications on Earth. Among the objectives are to develop, build and operate a multiorbital space-based state-of-the-art connectivity system, continuously adapted to governmental satellite communications demand evolution; to complement the Union pool of satellite communication capacities and services; and to integrate the GOVSATCOM ground segment infrastructure, as well as the European quantum communication infrastructure (EuroQCI).

In the context of the co-Programmed European Partnership for Globally Competitive Space Systems (Space Partnership), R&I will focus on cohesive activities in the domain of digital developments under the grand heading of Digitalisation for Commercial Space solutions, more specifically on collaborative and synergetic solutions for Earth Observation and Satellite Telecommunication missions.

  • Heading 4: Using Space on Earth related to Earth Observation

The evolution of Copernicus core services (Climate Change, Marine Environment Monitoring, Land Monitoring, Atmosphere Monitoring, Emergency Management and Security) is being taken care of through projects launched under the previous R&I work programmes.

In the context of the co-Programmed European Partnership for Globally Competitive Space Systems (Space Partnership), R&I will focus on cohesive activities in the domain of digital developments under the grand heading of Digitalisation for Commercial Space solutions, more specifically on collaborative and synergetic solutions for Earth Observation and Satellite Telecommunication missions.

In addition, we will strive to also support the development of innovative applications of Copernicus’ services and data. That said, such support is also coming from non-HE activities carried out by EUSPA, the EU agency for the Space Programme: collaboration with receivers’ manufacturers, with mobile phones’ manufacturers, with cars’ manufacturers, etc., as well as through influencing the development of policies where the use of Earth Observation data is required.

  • Heading 5: Using Space on Earth related to satellite navigation

For Galileo/EGNOS, the international context, the competitive environment with emerging actors including from the private sector, novel techniques in the value chain such as LEO layer for PNT or ground segment automation based on Artificial Intelligence, the increasing threats in space and in cyber, and the evolution of the technologies, components and systems, call for a constant adaptation of the EU space infrastructure to these changing realities.

To meet these challenges, EU needs sustained investments in R&D for innovative mission concepts, technology and systems. These will ensure the continuity of the EGNSS service, minimise the risks for technology inclusion in the infrastructure, thanks to anticipated development and testing including in-orbit, and protect better this infrastructure against modern threats (notably cyber, jamming/spoofing, natural hazards).

These investments in R&D will contribute to maintaining the EU´s leadership position in the Global Navigation Satellite Systems, and to strengthening the strategic autonomy of the EU.

In addition, we will strive to also support the development of innovative applications of EGNSS’ services and data. That said, such support is also coming from non-HE activities carried out by EUSPA, the EU agency for the Space Programme: collaboration with receivers’ manufacturers, with mobile phones’ manufacturers, with cars’ manufacturers, etc., as well as through influencing the development of policies where the use of satellite navigation data is required.

  • Heading 6: Space sciences and exploration

Space sciences and exploration are important areas that must be fostered for various reasons, focusing on where the EU can add value with limited financial means. Firstly, it is key to capitalise on Europe’s investments in space missions and exploit data coming from European space missions (including demonstration and validation). This should lay the grounds for future exploration missions. Furthermore, such focus on sciences will strengthen the position of leading European scientists and also animate societal interest in space. Last but not least, it will expand human knowledge and the natural curiosity of mankind.

  • Heading 7: Monitoring Space

Orbital space infrastructure, the data, and the services they deliver have become indispensable for European societies and economies and in the daily lives of Europeans. However, due to an increasingly congested orbital space, the likelihood of a satellite being severely damaged or destroyed in a collision has raised dramatically. Such risk calls for action to preserve European interests by protecting its private and public investments in space in a sustainable manner.

Based on the EU Space Programme, capabilities of the Space Situational Awareness (SSA) component and Space Surveillance and Tracking (SST) services are being developed and consolidated through a Partnership of 15 Member States. The EU SST Partnership Agreement has entered into force on 11 November 2022. With this Partnership, EU SST builds on the good results achieved by the initial consortium of 5 Member States and targets continuity of activities and service provision, improvement of specialisation on expertise, and consideration of the duality and security dimension of SST.

EU SST relies on the European industry, including start-ups, to develop and improve national, public-owned capacities based on Partnership’s requirements. In the pursuit of EU strategic autonomy, both as regards the need to protect EU space infrastructures and as regards the need to strengthen EU SST capabilities, research and development activities are aiming the enhancement and consolidation of EU SST autonomy in all orbital zones beyond the existing network of national assets, counting on MS contributions and leveraging complementary contributions from European private capabilities and commercial initiatives.

Importantly, SSA also covers the domains of Space Weather (SW) and Near-Earth Objects (NEO). For those domains, activities are ongoing and no additional ones are needed under the 2026-2027 WP.

  • Heading 8: Boosting space through EU non-dependence for key critical space technologies

Ensuring non-dependence for critical space technologies is key, especially in the current geo-political context. The European Commission has undertaken several activities and deployed new tools (e.g. the EU Observatory of Critical Technologies) for assessing space technologies and identify those that are critical from a dependency point of view. Within this domain, a number of technological developments will be initiated with focus on priorities stemming from on-going and planned EU Space missions, including IRIS2. Emphasis will be on reducing non-EU dependencies on critical space technologies across their whole supply chain from advanced materials to components, equipment, and sub-systems; providing unrestricted access to advanced space technologies relevant for EU space missions and programme components; developing or regaining capacity to operate independently in space by developing resilient space technologies supply chains, relying on EU supply chains and/or trustable and reliable supply chains not affected by non-EU export restrictions; enhancing competitiveness by developing products and capabilities reaching equivalent or superior performance level than those from outside the EU and compete at worldwide level; and opening new opportunities for manufacturers by reducing dependency on export restricted technologies.

  • Heading 9: Boosting Space through innovative space technologies

Mastering quantum technologies is essential for EU technological sovereignty and their use in EU space missions will offer major improvements in the performance of the EU space systems. Their developments will contribute to EU leadership in this field, in particular quantum sensing technology based on quantum accelerometers, developed in the frame of the Quantum Space Gravimetry pathfinder mission.

  • Heading 10: Boosting Space through IOD/IOV opportunities

IOD/IOV opportunities continue to be needed for experiments needing aggregation as well as for read-to-fly satellites. This includes the Flight Ticket Initiative to support competitiveness and innovation of the European Space sector.

  • Heading 11: Boosting Space through support to entrepreneurship

Business development, acceleration and upscaling of start-ups is also much needed, which has given rise to the set-up of the CASSINI Space Entrepreneurship Initiative. CASSINI provides support to business and innovation-friendly ecosystems, including the strengthening business skills in the space market segments and digital services based on space data. CASSINI also aims at making start-ups and scale-ups investment-ready and able to secure venture capital funding and at leveraging synergies with the InvestEU programme and the EU Space Programme.

  • Heading 12: Boosting Space through support to the Space Act and cybersecurity

The interinstitutional discussions for the adoption of an EU Space Act will start as soon as the Commission has issued its proposal still in 2025. One adopted, it will be important to foresee some studies and assimilated activities to support its implementation. The same goes for the area of cybersecurity which has become extremely important also in the Space domain.

Limiting participation in certain actions to Member States (and certain associated countries to Horizon Europe)

The Space research part of the Horizon Europe Programme is by default open to the world, promoting international cooperation to drive scientific excellence.

However, an important aspect of this Destination consists in ensuring security and strengthening strategic autonomy across key technologies and value chains, taking advantage of the possibilities that space offers for the security of the Union and its Member States. This objective requires special rules in specific cases to set the requisite eligibility and participation conditions to ensure the protection of the integrity, security and resilience of the Union and its Member States. Hence, on an exceptional basis and duly justified, this work programme may foresee a limited participation to entities from selected countries. Such exceptional circumstances would relate to prevalent considerations to safeguard the Union’s strategic assets, interests, autonomy or security. Possibilities for such limitations are framed by Article 22(5) of the Horizon Europe Regulation.

Legal entities established in China are not eligible to participate in both Research and Innovation Actions (RIAs) and Innovation Actions (IAs) falling under this Destination. For additional information please see “Restrictions on the participation of legal entities established in China” found in General Annex B of the General Annexes.

The following call(s) in this work programme contribute to this destination:

HORIZON-CL4-2026-03-SPACE

HORIZON-CL4-2027-03-SPACE

HORIZON-CL4-2027-EUSPA-SPACE

Expected Outcome:

The topic encompasses actions within the scope of the co-programmed European Partnership on Globally Competitive Space Systems (‘Space Partnership’) in the areas of satellite communication (SatCom), Earth Observation (EO) and New Commercial Space Transportation Solutions and is part of cohesive activities in the domain of digital developments under the grand heading of “digitalisation for commercial space solutions”.

Digitalisation is a major enabler for enhancing the value of an End-to-End EO and SatCom system. Under the area of Using Space on Earth related to SatCom and EO, below this topic focusses on the Low to Mid TRL level developments of key technologies[1] required to strengthen competitiveness in these domains with a dedicated focus on synergies between Earth observation and Satellite telecommunication technologies.

Projects are expected to contribute to one or several of the following outcomes:

  • Next generation Earth observation and SatCom payloads, technologies and processing means (on ground and in space);
  • Security of SatCom and EO services, supporting next-generation technologies for both ground and space commercial applications.

This will contribute to developing, deploying global, more flexible and reactive space-based services applications, to contribute to fostering the EU's space sector competitiveness, as stated in the expected impact of this destination.

Scope:

The areas of R&I, which needs to be addressed to tackle the above-mentioned expected outcomes are:

  • R&I on End-to-End SatCom Mission capabilities for increased robustness, energy efficient connectivity and compatibility with 5G & 6G waveforms such as constellation and network software management systems and optical communications, including both space and ground-based assets, and digital on-ground infrastructure to test and enhance operational efficiency;
  • R&I on building blocks and processes common to EO and SatCom systems allowing for in-orbit reconfigurability, faster data availability, on-board and on-ground smart computing and improved operation resilience.

Proposals are expected to promote cooperation between different actors (industry, SMEs, research institutions and infrastructures and academia) and consider opportunities to quickly turn technological innovation into commercial use in space.

It is expected that projects make use of existing EU technologies and/or building blocks, including at component level, contributing to EU non-dependence and strengthen competitiveness, and this should be clearly presented in the proposal. Furthermore, proposed activities should be complementary to H2020 and Horizon Europe funded projects, national activities and activities funded by the European Space Agency (ESA).

This topic contributes to the implementation of the European Partnership on ‘Globally Competitive Space Systems’ (GCSS).

In this topic, the integration of the gender dimension (sex and gender analysis) in research and innovation content should be addressed only if relevant in relation to the objectives of the research effort.

Online Manual is your guide on the procedures from proposal submission to managing your grant.

Horizon Europe Programme Guide contains the detailed guidance to the structure, budget and political priorities of Horizon Europe.

Funding & Tenders Portal FAQ – find the answers to most frequently asked questions on submission of proposals, evaluation and grant management.

Research Enquiry Service – ask questions about any aspect of European research in general and the EU Research Framework Programmes in particular.

National Contact Points (NCPs) – get guidance, practical information and assistance on participation in Horizon Europe. There are also NCPs in many non-EU and non-associated countries (‘third-countries’).

Enterprise Europe Network – contact your EEN national contact for advice to businesses with special focus on SMEs. The support includes guidance on the EU research funding.

IT Helpdesk – contact the Funding & Tenders Portal IT helpdesk for questions such as forgotten passwords, access rights and roles, technical aspects of submission of proposals, etc.

European IPR Helpdesk assists you on intellectual property issues.

CEN-CENELEC Research Helpdesk and ETSI Research Helpdesk – the European Standards Organisations advise you how to tackle standardisation in your project proposal.

The European Charter for Researchers and the Code of Conduct for their recruitment – consult the general principles and requirements specifying the roles, responsibilities and entitlements of researchers, employers and funders of researchers.

Partner Search help you find a partner organisation for your proposal.

Condizioni generali

1. Condizioni di ammissibilità: Limite e layout della pagina della proposta

Come descritto nell'allegato A e nell'allegato E degli allegati generali del programma di lavoro di Orizzonte Europa.

Limiti e layout della pagina della proposta: descritto nella parte B del modulo di domanda disponibile nel sistema di presentazione.

Il limite di pagine per la parte B dell'applicazione di ricerca e innovazione (RIA) utilizzando la somma forfettaria è di 45 pagine. Inoltre, è obbligatorio presentare una tabella di bilancio dettagliata, utilizzando il modello disponibile nel sistema di presentazione.

2. Paesi ammissibili

Come descritto nell'allegato B del programma di lavoro Allegati generali.

Alcuni paesi non appartenenti all'UE/non associati che non sono automaticamente ammissibili al finanziamento hanno previsto disposizioni specifiche per rendere disponibili i finanziamenti ai loro partecipanti ai progetti di Orizzonte Europa. Cfr. le informazioni contenute nella guida del programma Orizzonte Europa.

title: Integrità elettorale nel contesto digitale
destinationDetails:
Lo Stato di diritto, il rispetto dei diritti umani e la democrazia sono valori fondamentali dell'UE sanciti dall'articolo 2 del trattato sull'Unione europea. Questi valori forniscono all'Unione orientamenti di principio per far fronte agli inevitabili cambiamenti geopolitici economici, sociali e demografici che non potevano essere previsti al momento dell'elaborazione dei trattati. Ciò include il modo in cui la trasformazione digitale influenzerebbe il modo in cui il dibattito e i processi politici sarebbero modellati.

La democrazia è una pratica culturale tanto quanto un sistema politico. Si tratta di un punto di forza fondamentale delle società europee, che contribuisce a garantire il rispetto dell'uguaglianza, dello Stato di diritto, dei diritti fondamentali e della libertà. Gli attori con tendenze antidemocratiche attaccano le democrazie e le loro istituzioni perché la democrazia è una salvaguardia contro di loro [[Il rapporto 2025 del V-Dem Institute ("25 anni di autocratizzazione-democrazia Trumped?") conferma i segni, gli indicatori e le tendenze spaventosi catturati negli anni precedenti di misurazione: "La tendenza della "terza ondata di autocratizzazione" si sta approfondendo e diffondendo. Ciò include l'indebolimento della democrazia in alcune democrazie liberali consolidate, la rottura della democrazia in paesi che sono stati democratici per la maggior parte del XXI secolo, nonché l'approfondimento dell'autocrazia in Stati già autocratici […] Il declino democratico globale si approfondisce, indipendentemente da come affettiamo i dati e da quale misura utilizziamo" (pagg. 9 e 10)]. Anche le democrazie tradizionalmente ben funzionanti devono affrontare molte sfide, il che significa che devono anche adattarsi continuamente al mutare delle condizioni. La ricerca in scienze sociali e umanistiche (SSH) svolge un ruolo cruciale nella comprensione delle sfide e delle minacce attuali e nella mappatura dei percorsi futuri per soluzioni innovative. Basandosi su prospettive storiche, culturali, sociali, giuridiche e filosofiche, la ricerca promuoverà l'ulteriore sviluppo della democrazia al fine di rafforzare la partecipazione dei cittadini e l'elaborazione di politiche inclusive, promuovere l'uguaglianza e l'inclusività, affrontare l'impatto dell'IA e la trasformazione digitale della democrazia. Rafforzerà inoltre la resilienza democratica e la preparazione civica e preserverà il ruolo dei media liberi, indipendenti e plurali quali principi fondamentali della democrazia, tra gli altri obiettivi.

Impatto previsto:

Le proposte di temi nell'ambito di questa destinazione dovrebbero definire un percorso credibile per contribuire al seguente impatto previsto del piano strategico di Orizzonte Europa:

  • Rafforzare la governance democratica migliorando l'indipendenza, la responsabilità, la trasparenza, l'efficacia e l'affidabilità delle istituzioni e delle politiche basate sullo Stato di diritto e ampliando la partecipazione e l'impegno attivi e inclusivi dei cittadini, potenziati dalla salvaguardia dei diritti fondamentali.

L'obiettivo degli investimenti nella ricerca a sostegno di tale impatto è quello di sviluppare una solida base di conoscenze comprovate in grado di orientare l'elaborazione di politiche efficaci, pertinenti e ragionevoli, che rafforzino la resilienza dei sistemi democratici e li proteggano dalle minacce. Allo stesso tempo, cerca di promuovere il pensiero critico rafforzando nel contempo la fiducia dei cittadini nella democrazia, nelle sue istituzioni e nel senso più ampio possibile della partecipazione politica.

La destinazione cerca sinergie con altri programmi pertinenti dell'UE, in particolare per l'adozione dei risultati della ricerca e delle soluzioni innovative sviluppate nell'ambito di Orizzonte Europa. Si incoraggia l'interazione, tra l'altro, con i seguenti programmi: Europa digitale (DIGITAL), strumento di sostegno tecnico, CERV (Cittadini, uguaglianza, diritti e valori), Erasmus+, FSE+ e Europa globale: Strumento di vicinato, cooperazione allo sviluppo e cooperazione internazionale.

I richiedenti sono incoraggiati a prendere in considerazione, se del caso, i servizi offerti dalle attuali e future infrastrutture di ricerca europee finanziate dall'UE, in particolare quelle nel settore delle scienze sociali e umane [1]. Se del caso, le proposte dovrebbero sfruttare i dati e i servizi disponibili attraverso le infrastrutture di ricerca europee federate nell'ambito del cloud europeo per la scienza aperta, nonché i dati provenienti dai pertinenti spazi di dati.

Poiché la destinazione mira direttamente al coinvolgimento dei cittadini e a produrre cambiamenti duraturi, è di particolare importanza che le azioni di ricerca e innovazione promuovano i più elevati standard di trasparenza e apertura. Si dovrebbero compiere sforzi particolari per garantire che i dati prodotti nel contesto di questa destinazione siano FAIR (trovabili, accessibili, interoperabili e riutilizzabili). Se del caso, è incoraggiato ad aprire il processo, i criteri, le metodologie e i dati alla società civile nel corso della ricerca.

Per massimizzare l'impatto della R&Amp;I nell'ambito di questa destinazione, in linea con le priorità dell'UE, la cooperazione internazionale è incoraggiata ogniqualvolta sia pertinente nei temi proposti.

[1] Per un elenco completo cfr. https://ri-portfolio.esfri.eu/ri-portfolio/table. Nel settore delle scienze sociali, cfr. ad esempio: CESSDA - Consorzio degli archivi europei di dati sulle scienze sociali (https://www.cessda.eu/), ESS - Indagine sociale europea (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/), SHARE - Indagine sulla salute, l'invecchiamento e la pensione in Europa (https://www.share-eric.eu/ ) o sull'infrastruttura europea di ricerca sull'Olocausto (https://ehri-project.eu/)

descriptionByte:
Risultato atteso:

I progetti dovrebbero contribuire a tutti i seguenti risultati attesi:

  • I responsabili politici dell'UE, nazionali e locali possiedono le conoscenze necessarie per informare l'elaborazione di regolamenti, norme e strumenti elettorali che affrontano l'uso delle tecnologie digitali nelle elezioni e nelle campagne politiche, garantendone l'integrità, l'inclusività, l'accessibilità, l'equità, la trasparenza e la sicurezza.
  • Le organizzazioni coinvolte nei processi elettorali elaborano e attuano orientamenti per l'uso responsabile delle tecnologie digitali nelle elezioni e nelle campagne politiche, in linea con le normative dell'UE e nazionali.
  • Maggiore trasparenza e responsabilità nelle campagne politiche basate sull'IA, ottenute attraverso i requisiti per gli audit dei sistemi di IA, la divulgazione dei dati, la trasparenza per quanto riguarda gli algoritmi e le fonti dei modelli linguistici di grandi dimensioni (LLM) e lo sviluppo responsabile dell'IA.

Ambito di applicazione:

L'integrità dei processi elettorali in Europa si trova ad affrontare sfide nell'era digitale. La trasformazione digitale dei processi democratici ha creato nuove strade per il coinvolgimento dei cittadini, ma comporta anche rischi significativi derivanti dalla disinformazione per l'integrità dei processi elettorali e di altri processi democratici. Le preoccupazioni per le ingerenze straniere, esemplificate dalle attività della Russia, ma anche di altri paesi terzi, hanno sottolineato la necessità di misure solide per salvaguardare i processi elettorali, compreso il rafforzamento della cibersicurezza e della verifica degli elettori per prevenire la manipolazione elettorale percepita. Le piattaforme dei social media, in particolare, sono diventate campi di battaglia sempre più critici nella lotta per l'opinione pubblica, con strumenti basati sull'IA utilizzati per amplificare e diffondere artificialmente la disinformazione, manipolare il discorso pubblico e influenzare il comportamento degli elettori.

Per affrontare tali sfide, è essenziale esaminare gli effetti delle tecnologie digitali sull'opinione pubblica e sulla governance e studiare lo sviluppo dell'IA etica, della pubblicità politica trasparente e degli strumenti per contrastare la disinformazione, la disinformazione e la manipolazione delle informazioni e le ingerenze da parte di attori stranieri (FIMI). Ciò include l'esplorazione del potenziale delle tecnologie digitali per trasformare e migliorare i processi democratici, l'esame di approcci multipartecipativi, con particolare attenzione alla promozione del dialogo con le piattaforme online, i media e i partiti e movimenti politici, nonché il rafforzamento dei media tradizionali e nuovi e la garanzia di piattaforme alternative per migliorare la resilienza elettorale.

Le proposte dovrebbero inoltre esaminare i rischi che le nuove tecnologie comportano per l'integrità democratica, in particolare attraverso la manipolazione dell'opinione pubblica e dei processi elettorali, esplorando nel contempo i modi per sfruttare tali nuove tecnologie per comprendere meglio e mitigare tali minacce. Le proposte sono inoltre incoraggiate a esaminare in che modo i contenuti generati dall'IA attraverso i media, compresi i media di intrattenimento, influenzano l'opinione pubblica, le narrazioni sociali, gli stereotipi e le norme di genere e l'impegno civico. Inoltre, le proposte possono prendere in considerazione strategie per l'attuazione di misure crittografiche adeguate, compresa l'indagine di approcci basati sulla crittografia post-quantistica.

Le istituzioni dell'UE sono state attivamente impegnate ad affrontare le principali sfide per l'integrità elettorale, tra cui l'amplificazione artificiale della disinformazione, la responsabilità delle piattaforme online e la protezione dei processi democratici. Le proposte dovrebbero tenere conto delle iniziative politiche e strategiche in corso, in particolare il regolamento sulla pubblicità politica, la legge sull'IA, gli orientamenti elettorali della legge sui servizi digitali [1] e la raccomandazione della Commissione del 2023 su elezioni inclusive e resilienti, nonché il codice di condotta sulla disinformazione [2].

L'obiettivo finale è capire come creare sistemi elettorali solidi e resilienti in grado di affrontare le sfide dell'era digitale, garantire la sicurezza e l'integrità dei processi elettorali e promuovere elezioni libere, eque, inclusive, accessibili e trasparenti. A tal fine è necessario indagare sui rischi di attacchi informatici e ingerenze straniere nei processi elettorali, sviluppare strategie per migliorare la sicurezza del sistema di voto e promuovere la trasparenza elettorale, sviluppare sistemi di allarme rapido, strategie di sfatamento efficaci e misure di responsabilità per le piattaforme.

La ricerca dovrebbe avere un approccio interdisciplinare (comprese le discipline SSH), che riunisca una vasta gamma di portatori di interessi, tra cui, ma non solo, le autorità elettorali e altre autorità nazionali con responsabilità in materia elettorale, in particolare quelle rappresentate nella rete europea di cooperazione in materia elettorale, le organizzazioni della società civile, i media nuovi e tradizionali e le piattaforme digitali.

I progetti possono anche concentrarsi sul modo in cui la manipolazione delle informazioni e le ingerenze da parte di attori stranieri possono influenzare il discorso politico attraverso piattaforme digitali, in particolare durante i periodi elettorali, anche in modi che compromettono i diritti delle donne, delle persone LGBTIQ, delle persone con disabilità e di altri gruppi sottorappresentati. Ciò comporta anche l'esame della sicurezza dei processi elettorali, la protezione dell'integrità delle elezioni e il mantenimento della fiducia del pubblico nel processo democratico, con particolare attenzione a garantire la sicurezza e la protezione dei candidati politici, in particolare delle donne e delle persone LGBTIQ e di altri membri di gruppi minoritari, dalla violenza, dall'intimidazione e dalle molestie. Affrontare queste preoccupazioni richiede una comprensione globale di come l'IA modella le campagne politiche, le narrazioni dei media, l'impegno pubblico e la diffusione della disinformazione (di genere).

Le proposte sono incoraggiate a individuare altri progetti finanziati dall'UE relativi all'integrità elettorale nell'ambito del programma Orizzonte Europa (compresi, ma non solo, quelli nei settori della cibersicurezza e della ricerca e sviluppo dell'IA) e regimi di finanziamento complementari, come il programma Cittadini, uguaglianza, diritti e valori e il programma Europa digitale, e a esplorare potenziali opportunità di collaborazione con loro.

I richiedenti possono prendere in considerazione la partecipazione del Centro comune di ricerca (JRC) per sfruttare la sua vasta gamma di capacità scientifiche e tecniche, comprese le sue competenze in materia di tecnologie digitali, scienza dei dati e cibersicurezza, al fine di sostenere gli obiettivi dei progetti e migliorarne l'impatto complessivo.

Il manuale online è la guida sulle procedure, dalla presentazione delle proposte alla gestione della sovvenzione.

La guida del programma Orizzonte Europa contiene orientamenti dettagliati sulla struttura, il bilancio e le priorità politiche di Orizzonte Europa.

Funding & Tenders Portal FAQ - trovare le risposte alle domande più frequenti sulla presentazione delle proposte, la valutazione e la gestione delle sovvenzioni.

Servizio Ricerca - porre domande su qualsiasi aspetto della ricerca europea in generale e dei programmi quadro di ricerca dell'UE in particolare.

Punti di contatto nazionali (PCN) – ottenere orientamenti, informazioni pratiche e assistenza sulla partecipazione a Orizzonte Europa. Esistono anche PCN in molti paesi terzi e non associati ("paesi terzi").

Enterprise Europe Network – contattare il proprio referente nazionale EEN per una consulenza alle imprese, con particolare attenzione alle PMI. Il sostegno comprende orientamenti sul finanziamento della ricerca dell'UE.

Helpdesk informatico – contattare l'helpdesk informatico del portale Funding & Tenders per domande quali password dimenticate, diritti e ruoli di accesso, aspetti tecnici della presentazione delle proposte, ecc.

L'Helpdesk europeo per i DPI vi assiste in materia di proprietà intellettuale.

CEN-CENELEC Research Helpdesk e ETSI Research Helpdesk – le organizzazioni europee di normazione vi consigliano su come affrontare la normazione nella vostra proposta di progetto.

La Carta europea dei ricercatori e il codice di condotta per la loro assunzione – consultare i principi e i requisiti generali che specificano i ruoli, le responsabilità e i diritti dei ricercatori, dei datori di lavoro e dei finanziatori dei ricercatori.

Partner Search ti aiuta a trovare un'organizzazione partner per la tua proposta.

results.content: Första öppna ansökningsomgången – Stöd till små och medelstora företag inom textilsektorn i riktning mot en digital och grön omställning

beneficiaryAdministration:
Ansökningarna ska lämnas in uteslutande online via ansökningsportalen https://ec.europa.eu/eusurvey/runner/FutureProofTextiles-1st-OpenCall.

  1. Teknisk innovation (40 %): Bedöma den föreslagna lösningens nyhet, genomförbarhet och skalbarhet.
  2. Effekt & Hållbarhet (30%): Utvärderar bidraget till leveranskedjans resiliens, digitaliseringen och den gröna omställningen.
  3. Företagens bärkraft (20 %): Mäter marknadspotential, finansiell hållbarhet och kommersialiseringsstrategi.
  4. Genomförbarhet vid genomförandet (10 %): Granskar små och medelstora företags kapacitet, resursallokering och tidsplanen för genomförandet.

En internationell utvärderingskommitté med fem medlemmar som samordnas av UNIWA säkerställer en strikt konfidentiell och opartisk urvalsprocess, fri från nationella eller yrkesmässiga intressekonflikter. Ansökningarna bedöms rättvist mot officiella kriterier, med strikt efterlevnad av ESG-standarder och EU:s princip om att inte orsaka betydande skada. Dessutom måste de utvalda projekten aktivt integrera klimatneutrala metoder för cirkulär ekonomi och sträva efter jämställdhet på alla personalnivåer.
description:
Länk till den elektroniska ansökningsportalen: https://ec.europa.eu/eusurvey/runner/FutureProofTextiles-1st-OpenCall

Mål för öppen ansökningsomgång: Ge 20 små och medelstora företag inom textilsektorn möjlighet att framgångsrikt navigera i den digitala omställningens och den gröna hållbarhetens ”tvillingomställningar”.

Stöd: Utöver medfinansieringsbidraget på 60 000 euro (50 000 euro – schablonbidrag, 10 000 euro – obligatorisk självfinansiering från små och medelstora företag) erbjuder FutureProofTextiles omfattande kapacitetsuppbyggnads- och nätverksresurser för att bidra till att bygga upp ett sammankopplat ekosystem för små och medelstora företag:

  1. Skräddarsydd utbildning: I genomsnitt 40 timmar per litet eller medelstort företag med fokus på digital omvandling, principer för cirkulär ekonomi och hållbar produktion.
  2. Dedikerad mentorskap: Skräddarsydda tekniska konsult- och mentorsmöten för upp till sex utvalda små och medelstora företag baserat på särskilda behov.
  3. Material med öppen tillgång: Produktion av 100 timmar skalbara utbildningsplaner och guider för bästa praxis för den bredare textilsektorn.
  4. Gränsöverskridande nätverk: Underlättande av internationellt samarbete för att främja ett innovativt textilt ekosystem.

(Ytterligare information om dessa tjänster kommer att delas med de utvalda små och medelstora företagen.)

Vem kan ansöka:

Företagets storlek

  1. Sökande måste tillhöra kategorin små och medelstora företag, enligt Europeiska kommissionens rekommendation 2003/361/EG*
  2. Partnerskap Kluster och förmedlande organisationer är inte stödberättigade även om de är små och medelstora företag.
  3. Varje sökande bör företräda ett enda litet eller medelstort företag, inte ett konsortium av flera små och medelstora företag.

Näringsliv

  1. Sökande måste vara små och medelstora företag som är verksamma i värdekedjan för textilier. Små och medelstora företag från kompletterande sektorer (t.ex. teknik, maskiner) är också stödberättigade, förutsatt att deras föreslagna innovation direkt bidrar till värdekedjan för textilier. Verksamheterna måste överensstämma med en relevant Nace-kod (eller nationell motsvarighet), t.ex.
  2. Textiltillverkning: C13.1, C13.2, C13.3, C13.9
  3. Tillverkning av kläder: C14.1 och C14.3
  4. Textilbaserade produkter och tekniska textilier: C15.12 och C22.19
  5. Textilåtervinning och cirkularitet: C38
  6. Digitala och innovativa lösningar för textilsektorn: J62 och J63
  7. Tillverkning av maskiner för textil-, beklädnads- och lädertillverkning:C 28.94

Plats

  1. Endast små och medelstora företag som är lagligen etablerade i länder som deltar i programmet för den inre marknaden kan ansöka. Detta inbegriper EU:s medlemsstater och alla andra länder som formellt är associerade till SMP. En fullständig förteckning över de deltagande länderna finns här: Förteckning över länder som deltar i programmet för den inre marknaden

Språk

  1. Det ansökande SMF-företaget måste ha minst en anställd som talar engelska och kommer att vara aktivt involverad i genomförandeprocessen och hantera alla kommunikationsbehov med konsortiet.

Regler för inlämning:

Plattform

  1. Förslag som lämnats in online på EU:s undersökningsplattform. Andra medel kommer inte att accepteras. Ansökningsblankett

Språk

  1. Förslagen måste skrivas på engelska. Inlämningar som görs på något annat språk kommer inte att utvärderas.

Inlämningsgräns

  1. Sökande små och medelstora företag får lämna in upp till två förslag per öppen ansökningsomgång (ett inom grön omställning och ett inom digitala innovationer). Trots detta är varje litet eller medelstort företag berättigat till högst ett stipendium för hela programmet.

Krav på förslag

  1. Förslaget måste uppvisa en teknisk mognadsgrad (TRL) på 5 eller högre.

Efterlevnad & Etik

De sökande måste bekräfta att de till fullo följer alla regler, inklusive att det inte förekommer dubbelfinansiering och intressekonflikter, genom att granska och underteckna de obligatoriska formulär som ingår i ansökan:

  1. Formulär för anmälan av stödberättigande och avsaknad av intressekonflikt
  2. Formulär för anmälan av små och medelstora företag och stödberättigande

Steg för steg Guide

Sökande får lämna in ett förslag till ett projekt för grön omställning och ett till ett projekt för digital innovation. Observera att en separat ansökan måste lämnas in för varje ansökan.

Steg 1: Kontrollera behörighet

Granska behörighetskraven noggrant för att säkerställa att din organisation och projekt kvalificerar sig för finansiering.

Steg 2: Koncept & Budgetering

  1. Se dokumentet ”Uttömmande förteckning över stödberättigande verksamheter och stödberättigande kostnader”.
  2. Kolla in dokumentet ”Behoven hos små och medelstora företag i textilsektorn”, som hjälper till med brainstormingprocessen.
  3. Brainstorma ditt förslag. När du brainstormar, kom ihåg att projektets genomförandeperiod är 9 månader.
  4. Utarbeta ett första utkast och utarbeta en övergripande budget baserad på stödberättigande kostnader. Tydligt definiera dina mål genom att fastställa specifika milstolpar.

Steg 3: Utkast till svar

  1. Förbered dina svar för varje avsnitt i dokumentet ”Standardiserad mall för ansökningsformulär”, innan du börjar skicka in ansökan online.

Steg 4: Utarbeta obligatoriska dokument

Fyll i och underteckna följande obligatoriska formulär:

  1. Fyll i dokumentet ”Tabell med aktiviteter, budget, milstolpar och risker”. Observera att delmål kan bli föremål för förhandlingar om förslaget väljs ut, och sökande kommer inte att utvärderas på grundval av de föreslagna delmålen.
  2. Fyll i formuläret för försäkran om små och medelstora företag och stödberättigande.
  3. Fyll i formuläret ”Anmälan om stödberättigande och avsaknad av intressekonflikt”.

Steg 5: Fyll i onlineformuläret

Gå till webbportalen – EU Survey för att lämna in dina svar. Vi rekommenderar att du använder en stabil internetanslutning för att förhindra dataförlust.

Steg 6: Ladda upp bilagor

Bifoga alla obligatoriska dokument från steg 4 i respektive uppladdningsfält i formuläret.

Alla nödvändiga dokument finns tillgängliga för nedladdning via ansökningsportalen och genom relevanta inlägg i projekten LindeIn och ECCP-sidan.

  3. Viabilidade das empresas (20%): Mede o potencial de mercado, a sustentabilidade financeira e a estratégia de comercialização.

Coordenada pela UNIWA, uma comissão internacional de avaliação composta por cinco membros assegura um processo de seleção estritamente confidencial e imparcial, isento de conflitos de interesses nacionais ou profissionais. description:
Ligação para o Portal de Candidaturas em linha: https://ec.europa.eu/eusurvey/runner/FutureProofTextiles-1st-OpenCall

Objetivo do convite aberto em permanência: Capacitar 20 PME do setor têxtil para navegarem com êxito nas «duplas transições» da transformação digital e da sustentabilidade ecológica.

Apoio: Para além da subvenção de cofinanciamento de 60 000 EUR (50 000 EUR — subvenção fixa de montante fixo, 10 000 EUR — autofinanciamento necessário por parte das PME), a FutureProofTextiles oferece um amplo reforço das capacidades e recursos de ligação em rede para ajudar a construir um ecossistema de PME conectado:

  1. Formação à medida: Uma média de 40 horas por PME centrada na transformação digital, nos princípios da economia circular e na produção sustentável.
  2. Mentoria dedicada: Sessões personalizadas de consultoria técnica e mentoria para um máximo de 6 PME selecionadas com base em necessidades específicas.
  3. Materiais de Acesso Aberto: Produção de 100 horas de programas de formação moduláveis e guias de boas práticas para o setor têxtil em geral.
  4. Redes transfronteiriças: Facilitação da colaboração internacional para promover um ecossistema têxtil inovador.

(Outras informações relativas a estes serviços serão partilhadas com as PME selecionadas.)

Quem pode candidatar-se:

Dimensão da empresa

  1. Os candidatos devem enquadrar-se na categoria de PME, de acordo com a Recomendação 2003/361/CE da Comissão Europeia*
  2. Os agrupamentos de empresas e as organizações intermediárias não são elegíveis, mesmo que sejam PME.
  3. Cada candidato deve representar uma única PME e não um consórcio de várias PME.

Indústria

  1. Os candidatos devem ser PME que operam na cadeia de valor têxtil. As PME de setores complementares (por exemplo, tecnologia, maquinaria) também são elegíveis, desde que a inovação proposta contribua diretamente para a cadeia de valor têxtil. As atividades devem estar alinhadas com um código NACE relevante (ou equivalente nacional), tais como:
  2. Fabrico de têxteis: C13.1, C13.2, C13.3, C13.9
  3. Fabrico de vestuário: C14.1, C14.3
  4. Produtos têxteis e têxteis técnicos: C15.12, C22.19
  5. Reciclagem de têxteis e circularidade: C38
  6. Soluções digitais e inovadoras para o setor têxtil: J62, J63
  7. Fabricação de máquinas para a produção de têxteis, vestuário e couro:C 28.94

Localização

  1. Apenas as PME legalmente estabelecidas em países que participam no Programa a favor do Mercado Único (PMS) podem candidatar-se. Tal inclui os Estados-Membros da UE e qualquer outro país formalmente associado ao PMS. A lista completa dos países participantes é publicada aqui: Lista dos países participantes no Programa a favor do Mercado Único (PMS)

Língua

  1. A PME candidata deve ter, pelo menos, um membro do pessoal que fale inglês e participe ativamente no processo de execução, respondendo a todas as necessidades de comunicação com o consórcio.

Regras de apresentação:

Plataforma

  1. Proposta apresentada em linha na Plataforma de Inquérito da UE. Quaisquer outros meios não serão aceitos. Formulário de candidatura

Língua

  1. As propostas devem ser redigidas em inglês. As inscrições feitas em qualquer outra língua não serão avaliadas.

Limite de apresentação

  1. As PME candidatas podem apresentar até duas propostas por concurso público (uma no âmbito da transição ecológica e outra no âmbito das inovações digitais). Apesar disso, cada PME é elegível para receber um máximo de uma concessão de subvenção em todo o programa.

Requisitos da proposta

  1. A proposta deve demonstrar um nível de maturidade tecnológica (TRL) igual ou superior a 5.

Conformidade & Ética

Os candidatos devem confirmar a sua plena conformidade com todas as regras, incluindo a ausência de duplo financiamento e o conflito de interesses, revendo e assinando os formulários obrigatórios incluídos na candidatura:

  1. Formulário de declaração de elegibilidade do financiamento e de ausência de conflito de interesses
  2. Formulário de declaração de PME e de elegibilidade

Guia passo a passo

Os candidatos podem apresentar uma proposta para um projeto de transição ecológica e outra para um projeto de inovação digital. Chama-se a atenção para o facto de que deve ser apresentada uma candidatura separada para cada uma delas.

Etapa 1: Verificar elegibilidade

Reveja cuidadosamente os requisitos de elegibilidade para garantir que a sua organização e projecto se qualificam para financiamento.

Etapa 2: Conceito & Orçamentação

  1. Consulte o documento «Lista exaustiva de atividades elegíveis e custos elegíveis».
  2. Consulte o documento «Necessidades das PME no setor têxtil», que ajuda o processo de brainstorming.
  3. Faz um brainstorm à tua proposta. Durante o brainstorming, tenha em mente que o período de implementação do projecto é de 9 meses.
  4. Elaborar um projeto inicial e elaborar um orçamento abrangente com base nos custos elegíveis. Defina claramente os seus objetivos através do estabelecimento de marcos específicos.

Etapa 3: Projetos de respostas

  1. Prepare as suas respostas para cada secção do documento «Modelo normalizado de formulário de candidatura», antes de iniciar a apresentação em linha.

Passo 4: Preparar documentos obrigatórios

Preencha e assine os seguintes formulários necessários:

  1. Preencher o documento «Quadros com atividades, orçamento, etapas e riscos». Note-se que os marcos podem ser objeto de negociação se a proposta for selecionada e que os candidatos não serão avaliados com base nos marcos propostos.
  2. Preencha o «Formulário de declaração de PME e de elegibilidade».
  3. Preencha o «Formulário de declaração de elegibilidade do financiamento e de ausência de conflito de interesses».

Passo 5: Preencha o Formulário Online

Aceda ao portal em linha – Inquérito da UE para apresentar as suas respostas. Recomendamos a utilização de uma ligação estável à Internet para evitar a perda de dados.

Etapa 6: Carregar anexos

Anexar todos os documentos obrigatórios da etapa 4 nos respetivos campos de carregamento no formulário.

Todos os documentos necessários estão disponíveis para descarregamento através do portal de aplicações e através das publicações relevantes nos projetos LindeIn e na página do ECCP.
